summary: Sacks argues Nvidia's blowout quarter and 70% growth guidance (vs. 45% Street estimate) proves the AI CapEx boom has real legs, and that despite the 8% stock move the company trades at only 12x earnings — making it cheap relative to fundamentals.
quote: the fact that they guided to 70% growth next year, whereas the Street was only expecting around 45%. So that's pretty amazing. And that 70% number would've been higher, but they said they were supply constrained.

summary: Chamath argues Nvidia is building a vertically integrated stack — expanding from hardware into NeoClouds, models, APIs, and inference — which makes them a dominant force as the AI industry converges, and that at $1B/day in revenue their scale is extraordinary.
quote: A billion a day in revenue now.

summary: Chamath reaffirms his May call that Salesforce was meaningfully oversold, arguing that large horizontal systems of record hold a uniquely powerful position in the AI agent ecosystem because they own the contextual data enterprises need to train intelligent agents, driving strong net dollar retention and revenue growth.

summary: Friedberg argues from firsthand experience that horizontal platform companies like Salesforce are resilient to the AI disruption narrative because enterprises are better served building unique vertical workflows rather than rebuilding horizontal tools; Salesforce's breadth makes it the right system of record.
quote: the real SaaSpocalypse. It's more of a vertical SaaSpocalypse... Versus a platform like Salesforce. I totally agree with you.

summary: Chamath argues vertical SaaS companies — which own workflows rather than systems of record — are structurally vulnerable to AI disruption because they lack the canonical data moat that protects horizontal players like Salesforce, Workday, and Oracle.
quote: I don't think vertical SaaS has a system of record. I don't think that's what they do. I think they're workflows... I just wonder what survives.

summary: Friedberg argues there is no meaningful policy action Bessent can take to suppress long-end yields because the US has a structural fiscal spending problem; with $10T of debt to refinance in 12 months and borrowing costs at 5.2%, the bond market will continue to reprice US credit risk higher.
quote: there is no action that Bessent can take that's actually going to have a meaningful effect on the long end of the curve. We have fundamental fiscal spending problem with the federal government right now.
